source.name: SMS Spam Collection v.1
source.licence: Free to use with attribution to the authors' 2011 paper

corpus.split: 80/20, seeded, identical to spam-bench.json and features.json

models.name: The memoriser
models.how: Keeps every training message and its answer. Anything it has not seen before, it calls ordinary.
models.why: Nothing was learned about spam. The training score is a receipt for the filing, not a measure of skill.

models.name: Whichever message it looks most like
models.how: Keeps every training message and copies the answer of the one with the most words in common.
models.why: The other way to memorise. Its own training messages match themselves perfectly, so the training score is a hundred per cent and says nothing.

models.name: Flags everything
models.why: It catches all the spam, which sounds like success until you notice it catches everything else too. The same score on both halves, and useless on both.

models.name: Five hand-written rules, any of them
models.how: Flags a message if any of five reasonable rules fire.
models.why: Written by a person, so there is nothing to memorise and the two scores sit on top of each other. Rules do not overfit. They just are not very good.

models.name: The same model, on two hundred examples
models.how: The same naive Bayes, shown the first two hundred training messages.
models.why: Four times the examples, and it has begun to travel. Nothing about the method changed.

models.name: The same model, on a thousand examples
models.how: The same naive Bayes, shown the first thousand training messages.
models.why: Closing on the full model. The way to fix a model that has not learned enough is usually to show it more, not to make it cleverer.

models.name: Calls everything ordinary
models.why: Most messages are not spam, so doing nothing scores well on both halves. A high score is not evidence of anything on its own.

models.name: One hand-written rule
models.how: Flags anything containing a run of five or more digits.
models.why: A person wrote it, so there was nothing to memorise. It scores about the same on both halves, which is what a rule that generalises looks like.

models.name: Learned from the examples
models.how: Multinomial naive Bayes over the words, trained on the training half only.
models.why: It really did learn something transferable, and it still does a little better on the messages it studied. A small gap is normal and is not a scandal.

models.name: The same model, on fifty examples
models.how: The same naive Bayes, but shown only the first fifty training messages.
models.why: Too little to learn from, so it leans on whatever those fifty happened to contain. Small training sets produce confident models that do not travel.
